title: New study: de-notified tribes remain uncounted and over-policed seven decades after the Criminal Tribes Act was repealed
dek: A paper by two University of Delhi law researchers argues that the 1952 repeal changed the label, not the machinery, and asks for these communities to be counted in the 2027 Census.
body: Frontiers in Sociology published the paper "De-notified tribal communities and administrative exclusion in India" on 2 November 2026. Its authors, Lovenish Saini and Vidhi Madaan Chadda, are listed with the Faculty of Law, University of Delhi.

The colonial Criminal Tribes Act, first passed in 1871, declared whole communities criminal. It was repealed in 1952. The authors argue that the repeal removed the statute but left its working parts in place: surveillance registers, police history sheets and the idea of the "habitual offender", which lived on in state laws.

The study reads laws, prison manuals, court judgments, the reports of national commissions on De-notified, Nomadic and Semi-Nomadic Tribes and civil-society surveys; it does no new fieldwork. A central finding is that no arm of the state records de-notified status, so the census has no such category and these communities cannot be counted in crime or welfare data. The Renke Commission estimated their population at about 10.74 crore, extrapolated from the 2001 Census, and the Idate Commission identified about 1,262 communities.

Because there is no direct data, the authors rely on caste categories as a proxy and say their figures are indicative, not a national rate. They also note the Supreme Court's 2024 judgments against caste-based rules in prison manuals and against selective history-sheet entries.

Their recommendations: audit police and prison manuals line by line; tie any habitual-offender label to individual, reviewable findings; train police and prison staff in the history of the Act; involve community representatives; and enumerate de-notified, nomadic and semi-nomadic communities in the 2027 Census.
